verses.note: The one who crushes the serpent is himself wounded. The New Testament presents Christ's death as the defeat of the devil (Hebrews 2:14, Colossians 2:15), a victory won through being struck.

Noah comes before God on the far side of judgment by way of a sacrifice. The verse does not say what the offering accomplished, but in Israel's law the burnt offering was accepted “to make atonement” for the worshiper (Leviticus 1:4), and the new world's first act of worship takes that shape.

The promise follows directly on the LORD's smelling “the pleasing aroma” of the sacrifice. The verse ties God's decision to bear with the world to an accepted offering, a connection the New Testament uses when it calls Christ's death a fragrant offering to God (Ephesians 5:2).

Isaac's question, where is the lamb, is the question the whole sacrificial system will keep asking. Abraham's answer, that God will provide it, is taken up by John the Baptist when he names Jesus "the Lamb of God" (John 1:29).

The narrator describes Isaac with the vocabulary of an animal sacrifice. The reader is made to feel what a sacrificial death means when the victim is a beloved son. Isaiah 53:7 pictures the servant of the LORD led like a lamb to the slaughter, silent as Isaac is here.

The ram dies instead of Isaac. The principle of substitution, one life given in place of another, is stated here in its simplest form. The New Testament describes Christ's death with the same logic, the righteous for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18) and a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

The verse uses the vocabulary of atonement in its everyday sense: turning away a wronged party's anger by a costly gift. Israel's sacrifices would later use the same word, with the difference that God himself provides the means by which his face is turned toward his people (Leviticus 17:11).

The chapter never calls Jacob's gift a sacrifice, but it borrows the words for one: covering the face, the offering, the acceptance. Between people, as between God and people, the Old Testament knows that a wrong needs more than time to be put right. The chapter's grace, though, runs the other way: Esau's welcome comes before the gift is accepted.

Judah does not offer a substitute victim, as Reuben offered his sons (42:37). He puts himself under the liability. The verse is not a prophecy, but it is the first clear step toward the substitution of 44:33, where he asks to bear the penalty in Benjamin's place.

Judah offers his own freedom so that Benjamin may go free. This is substitution in the plainest sense, one taking another's place under a penalty, and Genesis uses the same preposition for the ram offered in Isaac's place (22:13). The New Testament does not cite this verse, but the pattern it shows is the one the gospel fulfills.

Blood stands between Moses' family and death, and the scene comes just before the Passover, where the blood on the doorposts will protect Israel's firstborn from the destroyer (12:13). Many interpreters see the night on the road as a small anticipation of that night.

The lamb that stands between the household and death has to be without defect. The same demand governs every sacrifice in Leviticus, and the New Testament applies it to Christ, who offered himself unblemished to God (Hebrews 9:14) and redeemed his people with blood like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19).

The blood stands between the household and the plague. Whether the Passover is classed with the atoning sacrifices or apart from them, the verse establishes that a life given in the house's place is what turns judgment away, the logic Leviticus 17:11 later states for all sacrificial blood.
The answer the children are given calls the rite a sacrifice. The Passover lamb is not merely food but a victim slain to the LORD, and the protection of the household is bound to its death.

The firstborn son is redeemed by a substitute. The law keeps alive the memory of the Passover night, when Israel's firstborn were spared (13:14-15), and establishes that a life claimed by God may be ransomed by a price he accepts.

Even the one who mediates atonement needs it. The priest's own sin offering comes first, a feature Hebrews singles out when it contrasts Aaron with a high priest who had no need to offer for himself (Hebrews 7:27).
The people's sin is dealt with by the same means as the priest's: blood brought before God. No one enters with the blood but the high priest, but the benefit belongs to the whole assembly (verse 17).

The day's work is double. The blood rite cleanses God's house; the live goat removes the people's guilt. Both are needed for God to go on dwelling among them, and the verse marks the hinge between them.

Sin is transferred and removed. The live goat is not killed; it carries guilt away where it can no longer touch the people. Psalm 103:12 and Micah 7:19 use similar pictures of distance and removal for God's forgiveness.

The goat bears the guilt of others. Isaiah 53 uses the same verb of the servant who bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and although the New Testament does not quote this chapter's goat directly, the language of one who carries away sin runs through its presentation of Christ (John 1:29; 1 Peter 2:24).

The day's result is cleansing ‘from all your sins’. Leviticus presents it as a real and complete provision for Israel's life with God in its time; Hebrews 10:1-4 and 10:11-14 argue that its yearly repetition showed it pointed beyond itself to a sacrifice that would need no repeating.

The day's power lay in God's appointment and in its annual return. Hebrews contrasts ‘once a year’ with ‘once for all’: the yearly rite recalled sins every year (Hebrews 10:3), while Christ appeared ‘once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself’ (Hebrews 9:26).

The verse explains why blood atones rather than simply asserting that it does: blood is life, and God has appointed life given up on the altar to cover the worshipers' lives. Whether that is best described as substitution, ransom, purification, or identification is debated among Christian and Jewish readers, but all agree the means of atonement is God's gift.
The prohibition protects the meaning of the altar. What God has set apart as the means of atonement cannot also be ordinary food, just as holy things in Leviticus cannot be used for common purposes.

Christians have long disagreed about what Jesus' use of this line means. Some stress that citing a psalm's opening evoked the whole psalm, including its vindication; others, including Luther and Calvin, held that Christ truly bore God's judgment on sin and experienced abandonment in his human soul; Jürgen Moltmann (The Crucified God, 1972) read the cry as God's own entry into godforsakenness. Classical theology adds that the Son's cry does not divide the Trinity; it is the true cry of his human nature bearing sin.

Whichever reading is right, the verse pictures the sufferer's hands and feet exposed to his attackers. Christian readers have seen in it the shape of the crucifixion, but the church's reading of Psalm 22 as a passion psalm rests on the Gospels' use of verses 1, 7-8, and 18, not on this verse alone.

The Gospels saw in this verse the literal dispossession of Jesus at his execution. The one who was stripped of everything is, in the psalm's movement, the one whose rescue brings the nations to worship.

A priest exists to draw near to God on behalf of others and to offer sacrifice. Hebrews argues from this verse that Christ's priesthood rests on an oath and an indestructible life, not on descent, and that he offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:16-17, 7:27).

The comfort rests on guilt dealt with, not ignored. Her iniquity is paid off, the language of Leviticus 26 for a debt settled. Isaiah 53 will say how God finally deals with iniquity: the LORD lays it on his Servant (53:6).

On the reading ‘sprinkle’, the Servant does for the nations what the priest did for Israel: he makes them clean. Hebrews speaks of hearts sprinkled clean (10:22) and of the sprinkled blood of Jesus (12:24), and 1 Peter 1:2 of sprinkling with his blood. On the reading ‘startle’, the atoning work is stated in chapter 53 rather than here. Either way, the song's opening already reaches beyond Israel to many nations.

The central claim of the song appears here: the Servant bears what belongs to others. The verse speaks first of sicknesses and pains, the effects of sin in human life, before verse 5 names transgressions and iniquities. The New Testament uses both halves: Matthew 8:17 applies this verse to Jesus' healings, and 1 Peter 2:24 applies verse 5 to his death.

The verse is the classic Old Testament statement of substitution: his suffering is caused by our transgression and produces our peace. Christians agree that the Servant's death is for others; they differ on how best to describe the mechanism. Penal substitution, defended for example by J. I. Packer's lecture What Did the Cross Achieve? (1974), stresses that the chastisement due to us fell on him. Christus Victor, the name Gustaf Aulén gave in 1931 to the patristic emphasis on Christ's victory over sin, death, and the devil, and representative or participatory accounts, stress his conquest and our union with him. Many theologians hold that the verse's language of punishment, healing, and peace needs more than one model to express it.

The Servant's silence is not weakness but consent. A lamb led to slaughter recalls the sacrificial lambs of Israel's worship, and John the Baptist's words, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29), may draw on this verse as well as the Passover. The Gospels note Jesus' silence before the high priest and Pilate (Mark 14:61, 15:5).

Only an innocent sufferer can bear the sins of others; one who deserved punishment would bear his own. The verse's plain statement of the Servant's innocence is the ground of verses 10 to 12. The New Testament affirms the same of Jesus: he committed no sin (1 Peter 2:22), he knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21).

The asham was the offering that dealt with a debt owed to God, paid with restitution. By naming the Servant's life an asham, the song interprets his death in the terms of Israel's sacrificial system, the move Hebrews makes at length (Hebrews 9:11-14, 10:10).

The verse promises atonement in the technical vocabulary of the sanctuary: lekhapper 'avon, ‘to atone for iniquity’. The end of exile is not enough; the prophecy looks to a final dealing with sin that the return from Babylon did not accomplish, which Christians identify with the cross (Hebrews 9:26).

The mourning of chapter 12 opens directly onto the promise of 13:1, a fountain opened for the house of David and Jerusalem to cleanse them from sin and impurity. Grief over the pierced one and cleansing from sin belong to the same day.
The prayer asks God to cancel the debt; the Gospel later says how, when Jesus calls his blood poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (26:28).

Jesus, who has no sin to confess, stands in the water with sinners. The early church read the baptism as the first step of his identification with those he came to save, which the cross completes (Isaiah 53:12, 2 Corinthians 5:21).

The cleansed man returns to the town, and Jesus is pushed outside to the places where the unclean lived. Many interpreters see in this exchange a small picture of what the cross will do: Jesus takes the outsider's place so that the outsider can come in (Hebrews 13:12-13).

Only a few pages into the Gospel, Jesus speaks of his own removal. The verse sets his death inside his mission from the start and makes the church's fasting a way of remembering that the bridegroom was taken, as early Christians did by fasting on Friday.

Jesus' exorcisms are the first signs of a victory completed at the cross, where, as Colossians 2:15 puts it, God disarmed the powers. Amillennial and postmillennial readers connect this binding with Revelation 20:2; premillennial readers see a fuller binding still to come.

The word must places Jesus' death inside God's purpose from the start of the passion teaching. The verse does not yet say why he must die; Mark answers that in 10:45 and 14:24. What it establishes is that the cross is not an interruption of his mission but its path.
If a person has nothing to give in exchange for his soul, redemption must come from outside him. The question prepares for 10:45, where Jesus gives his life as the ransom no one else could pay.

The Son of Man is handed over, a word that in the passion story names human betrayal and in Isaiah and Paul names God's own giving of his Son. Mark lets both be heard: sinful men do their will, and God's purpose stands behind the handing over.

The verse teaches that Jesus' death was the purpose of his coming and that it was a ransom given in place of many. Christians have drawn on it for several models of the atonement: the fathers who spoke of a ransom paid to free humanity from bondage (Origen and Gregory of Nyssa pressed the question of to whom), and later theologians who stressed substitution and satisfaction. The text itself names the price (his life), the beneficiaries (many), and the relation (in their place), without saying to whom the price was paid.

Poured-out blood is sacrificial language (Leviticus 4:7), and ‘for many’ recalls the servant who ‘bore the sin of many’ (Isaiah 53:12). The verse joins the ransom saying of 10:45 with the covenant: Jesus' death is the sacrifice by which a people is bound to God and its sin borne.

‘I will strike’ puts the cross within God's own action. The New Testament will say God did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all (Romans 8:32); the striking of the shepherd is for the sake of the flock.

In the prophets the cup is the cup of God's wrath poured out on the nations and on Jerusalem (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus' dread is not only of pain but of drinking that cup, the judgment he takes in his people's place.

Barabbas, a murderer, is set free because Jesus is condemned. Mark draws no lesson from it, but Christian readers from early on have seen the whole shape of substitution in the exchange: the one who deserved death walks out, and the innocent one dies in his place (1 Peter 3:18).

The Son who called God Abba in Gethsemane now says only ‘my God’, and asks why. Christian theology has read the cry as Jesus entering the separation from God that sin brings, bearing the curse in his people's place (2 Corinthians 5:21, Galatians 3:13), while holding that the eternal union of Father and Son was not dissolved.
Mark reports the death itself in two words, exepneusen, ‘he breathed his last’. The creeds' ‘was crucified, died, and was buried’ rests on the plainness of this verse: the Son of God really died.

The curtain marked separation between a holy God and sinners, crossed once a year with blood. Its tearing at the moment of Jesus' death says his death achieves what the Day of Atonement pointed to (Hebrews 9:11-12).

The sinless one receives a baptism of repentance among ‘all the people’. The church has read this as his first act of standing with sinners, the solidarity that leads to the cross, where he is counted among the lawless (22:37).

The offerings Jesus sends the man to present include sin and guilt offerings by which the priest ‘makes atonement’. Luke's readers see in the one who cleanses the reality those sacrifices pointed toward.

Jesus forgives before the cross, on his own authority. Luke will show that the same Son of Man must suffer (9:22) and that forgiveness is preached in his name because he suffered and rose (24:46-47): the authority and the atonement belong together.
The bridegroom will be ‘taken away’. In a scene about feasting, Jesus quietly announces that his presence will end in violent removal, the first shadow of the cross in Luke.

The elders, chief priests, and scribes were the three groups that made up the Jerusalem council, so Jesus foretells an official rejection by Israel's leaders. Luke's dei places that rejection inside God's purpose, the necessity he will later explain from Moses and the Prophets (24:26-27, 46).

Jesus' death is called an exodus to be fulfilled. The word frames the cross, and with it the resurrection and ascension, as the new act of deliverance for God's people, as the first exodus was Israel's rescue from slavery. Luke does not explain the mechanism here, but he names the event in the language of redemption.

The second prediction is shorter than the first and centers on one word, ‘handed over’. Human hands will do it, Judas and the council and Pilate, and yet the verb also belongs to Isaiah's servant whom the LORD gives up for others, so Luke's readers can hear both human betrayal and divine purpose in it.

The suffering is not an accident that God overcame. Jesus says it was necessary, which is Luke's way of saying the cross belongs to God's saving purpose, the purpose Jesus had named at the Supper when he spoke of his body given and blood poured out (22:19-20).

John's words say that Jesus deals with sin by removing it, and that he does so as a lamb, an animal of sacrifice. The verse does not spell out a theory of how the removal happens; the Gospel's account of the cross at Passover and Isaiah's servant who bears sins supply that.

The first mention of Jesus' hour comes at a wedding table, and every later use points to his death (12:23-27, 13:1, 17:1). By joining the hour to a lack of wine, John lets the reader see that the joy Jesus gives at Cana is drawn on the account of the cross, where the hour arrives.

The zeal that clears the temple is the zeal that will consume Jesus. By changing the psalm's past tense to a future, John makes the quotation a prophecy of the passion: the temple act leads to the cross, as the Synoptic Gospels show when they place it in the last week.

The comparison ties salvation to the cross. The Israelites were dying under judgment for their own rebellion, and God provided the remedy in the very form of what was killing them. The Son of Man, lifted up in death, is the remedy for sin's deadly bite.

John introduces Jesus as the Lamb of God (1:29) and will have him die as the Passover lambs are slaughtered (19:14, 19:36). Setting the bread of life discourse at Passover prepares the reader to hear the flesh ‘given for the life of the world’ (6:51) as sacrificial language.

The bread is not only the Son who came down but the flesh he will give up in death, and it is given huper, for the life of the world. The verse moves the discourse from incarnation to sacrifice: life comes to the world through the gift of Jesus' body in death.

The shepherd's death is for the sheep, on their behalf. John does not yet say how the death saves, but the preposition huper and the link to 11:50-52 show a death that benefits others and that God intends for their gathering and life.

Jesus' death is not something done to him against his will. It is a free act, under the Father's charge and with his own authority, which is why the Gospels can say both that he was handed over and that he gave himself (Galatians 2:20).

Caiaphas states, without meaning it, the logic of substitution: one dies so that many do not perish. The same words that express political expedience express God's purpose, which is why John can call them prophecy in the next verse.

Jesus' death is ‘for’ (huper) the nation and for the scattered children of God. Its purpose is not only to rescue individuals but to gather a people, which makes the cross the foundation of the church's unity.

Jesus' death is not a loss that interrupts his work but the means of its fruitfulness. The single grain becomes a harvest of many, which fits Isaiah's promise that the servant who pours out his life will see his offspring (Isaiah 53:10-11).

The cross is a victory as well as a sacrifice. The ruler of this world is cast out at the moment he seems to triumph, a theme Paul states when he says God disarmed the powers and triumphed over them in the cross (Colossians 2:15).

The lifted-up Son becomes the center toward which people are drawn. The cross is not only something done for the world at a distance; it is the power that brings people to Christ, as the bronze serpent drew the eyes of the dying in the wilderness (3:14, Numbers 21:8-9).

John presents Jesus' death as an act of love and obedience toward the Father, not a defeat forced on him. The world is meant to learn from the cross that the Son loves the Father, as it learns from the same cross that God loved the world (3:16).

Jesus speaks of his own death, hours away, as love laying down its life on behalf of others. Paul pushes the thought further when he says Christ died for us while we were still sinners and enemies (Romans 5:6-10); the two statements belong together, since the friends of this verse are those Jesus has made his friends, including a Peter who will deny him.

Jesus speaks of his death as a victory over the world. Gustaf Aulén (Christus Victor, 1931) argued that this theme of Christ's triumph over the powers of sin, death, and the devil was the classic view of the atonement in the early church, and the verse is one of its texts. Other accounts of the atonement, which stress sacrifice and substitution, do not deny the victory but explain it by what the cross accomplished for sinners.

The disciples' holiness rests on Christ's self-offering. Hebrews uses the same perfect participle: by God's will we have been sanctified (hēgiasmenoi) through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Hebrews 10:10).

The pattern of the cross appears in miniature: the one is taken and the many are released. John does not explain the atonement by this scene, but he places it at the start of the passion so that the reader sees the shape of what follows.

The cup in the prophets is often God's judgment poured out for the nations and for Jerusalem to drink (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus calls it the cup the Father has given him and refuses to let Peter's sword stand between him and it: he goes to drink what others deserved.

Caiaphas meant a political calculation: sacrifice one troublemaker to protect the nation from Rome. John reads his words as unwitting prophecy (11:51-52). One man does die for the people, and the preposition huper carries the Gospel's language of substitution.

The accusers guard their ceremonial purity in order to eat the Passover while handing over the one John called the Lamb of God (1:29). The irony is John's way of saying that the true Passover is being prepared in the very act they think is incidental to it.

A man guilty of violence goes free and the innocent one remains bound. John does not comment, but the exchange enacts on the human level what the cross does: the guilty released because another is condemned in his place.

John places the sentence at the hour when the Passover proper began and the lambs were about to be slaughtered. Whatever the harmonization of the calendars, John wants his reader to see Jesus' death as the Passover sacrifice that frees God's people (1 Corinthians 5:7).
The crowd's ‘take him away’ uses the verb of 1:29. Unknowingly they ask for the removal of the one who removes the world's sin, and he is taken away so that sin may be.

Hyssop, which applied the blood of the Passover lamb to the doorposts in Egypt (Exodus 12:22), lifts the wine to the lips of the Lamb of God. The detail is small and deliberate: John keeps Passover in the reader's mind at the moment of death.

The work the Father gave the Son is complete, and the perfect tense says it remains complete. Nothing is left undone that must be added for sin to be taken away; the Reformers made this word central to their teaching that Christ's sacrifice was once for all (Hebrews 10:12-14).

The pierced side gives the Gospel's clearest witness that Jesus truly died, and the flow of blood and water points to what his death gives: cleansing and life, the streams of living water promised in 7:38-39 and the fountain for sin of Zechariah 13:1.
By applying the Passover law to Jesus' body, John makes his death the true Passover sacrifice, the death by which God's people are spared and set free (1 Corinthians 5:7).

By saying the crucifixion was planned by God, Peter tells the crowd that Jesus' death was not a failure or accident but the center of God's saving purpose, as Luke 24:26 had said: the Messiah had to suffer.

Redemption is a costly release. Paul does not say here to whom a price is paid; the image stresses freedom from bondage at a cost, which Mark 10:45 and 1 Peter 1:18-19 connect with Christ's life and blood.

Three readings of hilastērion are held. Propitiation, the turning away of God's wrath, was defended by Leon Morris (The Apostolic Preaching of the Cross, 1955) and Roger Nicole, who point to the wrath of 1:18 and 2:5. Expiation, the cleansing or covering of sin, was argued by C. H. Dodd (The Bible and the Greeks, 1935) from Septuagint usage. The mercy seat reading, argued by Daniel Bailey and others, sees the place of atonement itself. Many interpreters hold that Paul's image includes both the removal of sin and the satisfaction of God's justice, since verse 26 names the problem as God's own righteousness.

The cross is where God's justice and mercy meet. Christians describe how in different ways (penal substitution, satisfaction, the victory of Christ, the demonstration of love), and the chapter note sets them out; the verse insists that whatever happened there, it vindicated God's righteousness.
Christ's death dealt with our trespasses. The passive verb leaves God as the one who handed him over, as 8:32 says outright, so that the cross is God's own saving act, not an event forced on him.
Christ died on behalf of the ungodly. The phrase ‘for the ungodly’ explains how the God of 4:5 can justify them: the one who died took their place, at the time God appointed.
Because the cross demonstrates God's own love, no account of the atonement can set a loving Son against an unwilling Father. The Father gave, and the Son gave himself (8:32, Galatians 2:20).
Reconciliation was accomplished through the Son's death while people were still enemies. God did not wait for his enemies to seek peace; he made it from his side, at his own cost.
Reconciliation is received as a gift. The believer contributes nothing to the peace except receiving it, which is why boasting now rests in God alone.
One righteous act undoes the effects of one trespass. The atonement is not only the removal of guilt but the reversal of Adam's story by a second head of humanity whose obedience brings life.

‘Once for all’ marks Christ's death as unrepeatable and complete. Hebrews uses the same word for his single offering (Hebrews 7:27, 9:12, 10:10). Believers do not re-enact his death; they share in its effect.

The verse is one of Paul's clearest statements that Christ's death was a sin offering in which God passed sentence on sin. The condemnation believers escape (verse 1) is the condemnation God executed on sin in Christ's flesh.

God gave his Son up ‘for us all’. The initiative in the cross is the Father's, and his giving is the measure of his love. Paul uses the same verb for Christ giving himself (Galatians 2:20), so the Son's self-offering and the Father's giving are one act.

The first article of the earliest creed is not only that Christ died but that he died ‘for our sins’. His death is interpreted from the start as dealing with sin, and interpreted by Scripture, not invented after the fact to explain a disaster.

Verse 17 ties forgiveness to the resurrection. The cross is not effective as a bare event; the resurrection is God's declaration that the death for sins succeeded (compare Romans 4:25, ‘raised to life for our justification’).
Paul speaks of the cross in the first person singular: the Son of God loved ‘me’ and gave himself for ‘me’. The death that was for our sins (1:4) is also a personal act of love for each believer.

The necessity of the cross proves the insufficiency of the law. If law-keeping could make a person right with God, Christ's death would be pointless; its reality is the measure of what the law could not do.

The curse that belonged to the law's transgressors fell on Christ, and he bore it ‘for us’. This is one of the plainest statements of substitution in Paul: the cross was an exchange of curse for blessing (verse 14).

Redemption is ‘through his blood’: Christ's death is the price of release, and forgiveness is what it secures. Colossians 1:14 has almost the same words, one of many close parallels between the two letters.

Nearness to God is achieved by blood, the language of sacrifice. What the temple sacrifices symbolized, access to God's presence, Christ's death accomplishes for those who had no right to approach the temple at all.
Peace with God and peace between peoples are one work. Christ is the peace, so reconciliation is not a program the church adds to the gospel but part of what the cross accomplished.

The verse says reconciliation is ‘to God’ first. Hostility between people and God (verse 3's wrath) is dealt with at the cross, and because both groups are reconciled to the same God, they are reconciled to each other.

The hymn presents Christ's death first as obedience. Paul elsewhere draws out that this obedience reverses Adam's disobedience (Romans 5:19), and here it becomes the ground of his exaltation in verse 9.
Redemption is located in the Son (‘in whom’) and defined as forgiveness. The blood is not named here, but verse 20 and the parallel in Ephesians 1:7 connect this redemption to Christ's death.

The cross is the means of reconciling not only individuals but ‘all things’. Christian readings differ on the scope. Origen and later universalists took it as the eventual restoration of all, including fallen powers; most interpreters, noting 2:15, read it as the pacification of the powers, brought back under God's rule by defeat rather than by salvation. All agree the verse ties the whole creation's healing to the cross.
Reconciliation happens in Christ's body of flesh through death. The physical, historical death of Jesus, not a spiritual ascent or an angelic mediator, is where God made peace.

Purification for sins is placed between the Son's eternal identity and his enthronement. The sacrifice is described as finished, and the seated posture, which chapter 10:11-12 will contrast with priests who stand daily, is the sign of that completion.

Jesus tasted death ‘for’ (huper, on behalf of) everyone. Christians differ on the extent this implies: Arminian and many Lutheran readers see a death offered for all people, while Reformed readers such as John Owen (The Death of Death in the Death of Christ, 1647) read ‘everyone’ in the light of the ‘many sons’ of verse 10. All agree it was a substitutionary death undertaken by God's grace.

Christ's death disarms the devil and frees people from fear of death. This is the victory theme of the atonement, which Hebrews sets beside the priestly theme of verse 17 without choosing between them.
Atonement is a priestly act performed by one who shares the nature of those he represents. The verse joins incarnation and atonement: the priest had to be one of the people.

The whole Levitical system assumed that the mediator himself needed atonement. That fact becomes the author's argument: a priest who must offer for his own sins cannot finally deal with anyone else's, and Hebrews will present Christ as the priest who offers for others alone.

The salvation Christ causes is ‘eternal’ because the priest who secures it has completed his work and holds office forever. Hebrews will spell out what that completed work was in 9:12, 9:14, and 10:14.
Christ is both priest and victim. Because he had no sins of his own, his offering could be wholly for others, and because he offered himself, not an animal, it needed no repeating.
Christ's priesthood is not an honorary title. A priest must offer, and Christ's offering is the center of his priestly work, which the next two chapters identify as the gift of himself.
The new covenant's deepest promise is complete forgiveness, sins no longer held against the sinner. Hebrews will argue that only a final sacrifice could make such a promise true (10:14-18).

The hilastērion was the place where atonement was made, the meeting point of God's presence above and the covenant tablets below. Paul applies the word to Christ (Romans 3:25), and Hebrews will show Christ fulfilling the rite performed there.
Christ's offering is his own life, not an animal's, and its effect is ‘eternal’. The Day of Atonement had to be repeated every year; the redemption Christ secured does not expire.
Christ's blood cleanses the conscience, the inner place the old sacrifices could not reach (verse 9). The atonement deals with guilt before God, not only with ritual status.

Christ's death covers sins committed before it. The saints of the old covenant were forgiven on the credit of a sacrifice still to come, which is how Paul speaks of God passing over former sins in Romans 3:25.
The ‘covenant’ reading adds a strong substitutionary note: the death required is the death that the covenant curse demands of those who broke it, borne by Christ on their behalf.

‘Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness’ states the logic of the whole sacrificial system: life for life, as Leviticus 17:11 teaches. Hebrews does not say God is bound by the rite but that the rite taught a truth about sin that Christ's death fulfills.

Christ's sacrifice reaches beyond the individual conscience to the whole order of access to God. Whatever the precise sense, the verse makes his offering the ground on which heaven itself is opened to sinners.

The sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice is measured by its singularity. A sacrifice that had to be repeated would be proved inadequate by its repetition; one offering at the climax of history is enough for sin from the foundation of the world.
A sacrifice that has to be repeated leaves the conscience unresolved. Christ's single offering makes possible a conscience no longer burdened with the question of whether sin has been dealt with.

Animal blood could not take away human sin. The sacrifices were God's appointed signs, effective for ritual cleansing and the covenant's ongoing life, but the reality of atonement required a human offering and a perfect one.
The offering of Christ's body fulfills the will of God that sacrifices could not. The atonement is at once an act of obedience and an act of sacrifice, the obedient Son giving his body.
The contrast of standing and sitting makes the letter's argument visible: many sacrifices that never finish, one sacrifice that is complete.
Complete forgiveness ends the need for further offering. The finality of Christ's sacrifice is the ground of assurance: nothing remains to be paid.
Christ's death opens a way into God's presence for all his people. The access once limited to one man, one day a year, now belongs to every believer, by the blood of Jesus.

The ground of victory over Satan is the Lamb's blood. The accuser loses because Christ's death has answered the charges he brings; the verse ties the atonement directly to the defeat of evil, not only to the forgiveness of sins.
